With such a small n, differences of only a few points (e.g., SFT+GRPO 48.75% vs SFT+RC-GRPO 46.25% on Qwen2.5-7B, a swing driven by just 2 out of 80 examples) cannot be distinguished from sampling noise without additional statistical treatment, yet the paper repeatedly frames such differences as substantive evidence for or against components of the method (e.g., Q1–Q2 analyses).
* Quote: "Table 1 reports accuracy on BFCLv4 (overall and by category)."
   * Comment: The by-category breakdowns (Base, Miss Func, Miss Param, Long Context) further subdivide the already-small 80-example test set into even smaller subgroups (17–23 examples each per Table 7), making category-level comparisons even less statistically reliable, yet these subcategory numbers are used to support fine-grained claims about where the method helps.

## Item 2: Overclaiming "surpasses all closed-source API models" from an unfair, non-comparable evaluation setup

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper's central claim that its fine-tuned open-weight model "surpasses all closed-source API models" compares a model that was explicitly SFT- and RL-trained on the exact BFCLv4 training distribution (including task-specific failure/success trajectories) against API models that are presumably evaluated without any such task-specific fine-tuning, which is common practice for closed-source models accessed only via API. This asymmetry is not disclosed or discussed, making the conclusion about API models potentially misleading.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions/data interpretation robustness; Clarity and context.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "our method even surpasses all closed-source API models" (abstract), and "the best-performing closed API baseline in Table 1 achieves 61.25% overall accuracy, which remains below our best open-weights result (85.00% on Qwen2.5-7B)."
   * Comment: The paper never states whether the API models were fine-tuned on the same 720 in-distribution training examples used for the open-weight models, or evaluated purely zero-shot/few-shot; given that closed API models generally cannot be fine-tuned by external users on a custom dataset the way the open-weight Qwen/LLaMA models were here, the comparison likely pits a task-specialized model against generalist models, so the claim of "surpassing" is not an apples-to-apples comparison and should be qualified.
* Quote: "In addition, we report BFCLv4 validation accuracy for several closed API models (Opus-4.5, Sonnet-4.5, GLM-4.7, Gemini-3-Pro, GPT-5.2) evaluated under the same API-calling setting."
   * Comment: "Same API-calling setting" only clarifies that the interaction protocol (turn-taking, tool call format) is matched, not that the models are matched in terms of training exposure to the benchmark's exact questions and ground truth-derived failure trajectories, which is the actual confound relevant to the "surpasses" claim.

## Item 3: Statistically invalid significance testing on autocorrelated training-step time series

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper reports p-values for Pearson correlation between entropy and training reward computed across sequential training steps within a single run, treating these steps as independent samples. Training-step metrics (entropy, reward) are highly autocorrelated over time, which is well known to invalidate standard significance tests that assume i.i.d. observations, inflating apparent significance.
* Evaluation criteria: Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Here, ρ denotes the Pearson correlation coefficient computed across training steps between the logged entropy values and the logged training reward values (no smoothing)."
   * Comment: Because entropy and reward evolve smoothly and autocorrelate strongly across adjacent training steps (they are not independent draws), the effective sample size for testing correlation significance is far smaller than the nominal number of training steps, so the reported significance levels are very likely overstated.
* Quote: "***: p < 0.001, **: p < 0.01, n.s.: not significant." (Table 4 caption)
   * Comment: Presenting formal significance markers derived from a single training run's time series, without accounting for autocorrelation (e.g., via block bootstrap, effective sample size correction, or multiple independent runs), gives an unwarranted appearance of statistical rigor to what is essentially a qualitative trend observation from one run per method.

## Item 4: Failure-trajectory dataset generated by one model (Qwen2.5-7B) is reused to fine-tune a different model (LLaMA-3.1-8B), confounding the RCTP mechanism

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The mixed-quality dataset used to train the Reward-Conditioned Trajectory Policy (RCTP) relies on failure trajectories collected from rollouts of one specific model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), but this same dataset appears to be used to fine-tune the differently-architected LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct model as well, without a model-specific failure trajectory set. This means the "low reward" mode learned by LLaMA-3.1-8B may not reflect its own natural failure modes, undermining the interpretability of the RCTP mechanism and the fairness of the LLaMA-3.1-8B results.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology transparency; Validity.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Failure Trajectories (800): Collected via RL exploration rollouts using Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. These capture diverse failure modes including incorrect tool selection, parameter errors, and premature termination."
   * Comment: This description appears in the general "Data Curation Pipeline" section (B.1.1) without any indication that a separate failure-trajectory collection was performed for LLaMA-3.1-8B, suggesting the same Qwen-generated failure set may have been reused across both base models; since RCTP-FT is explicitly designed to teach a model to "generate systematically different-quality trajectories under different tokens" based on its own error distribution, training on another model's failure modes could weaken the conditioning signal specifically for LLaMA-3.1-8B, potentially explaining its comparatively smaller gains (48.75% vs Qwen's 85.00%) but this confound is neither disclosed nor discussed.
* Quote: "In practice, D is curated by combining expert (successful) trajectories from the benchmark ground truth with diverse failure trajectories generated by exploration rollouts, and then injecting the appropriate reward token into each example; see Appendix B for full details."
   * Comment: The main text is vague about whether "exploration rollouts" are model-specific, and Appendix B.1.1 only explicitly names Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct as the rollout source, leaving the reproducibility and validity of the LLaMA-3.1-8B experimental pipeline unclear.

title: VLAW: Iterative Co-Improvement of Vision-Language-Action Policy and World Model
review:
## Item 1: Insufficient statistical rigor in success-rate evaluation

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper reports single-run success rates across only 40–50 real-robot trials per task with no repeated trials, confidence intervals, or variance estimates, making it impossible to assess whether the reported improvements are statistically meaningful rather than noise.
* Evaluation criteria: Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties; Conclusions.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "All task is evaluated 50 times since we collect 50 online rollouts in each iteration. DSRL baseline is evaluated with 10 times since it's too time-consuming to evaluate too many rollouts during online update."
   * Comment: With only 50 (or 10 for DSRL) binary trials, the standard error on a success rate near 0.5 is roughly ±7 percentage points, meaning many of the reported task-level differences in Table 2 (e.g., 0.80 vs 0.72 for Scooping) fall within noise. The paper presents these single-point estimates in Figure 7 and Table 2 without any error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed repetitions, despite drawing strong conclusions such as "VLAW consistently outperforms both the filtered BC and DSRL baselines." Given that the entire training pipeline (world-model fine-tuning, reward-model fine-tuning, policy fine-tuning) is stochastic, running each condition only once and evaluating with such small trial counts is insufficient to substantiate claims of consistent superiority. Common practice in robot-learning papers making comparable claims is to report multiple training seeds and/or larger evaluation trial counts with confidence intervals.

## Item 2: Unfair comparison between baselines due to unequal evaluation budgets

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The DSRL baseline is evaluated with only 10 rollouts while all other methods (including the proposed method) are evaluated with 50 rollouts, which introduces an evaluation asymmetry that biases the comparison and undermines the validity of the reported baseline comparison.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity; Conclusions.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "DSRL baseline is evaluated with 10 times since it's too time-consuming to evaluate too many rollouts during online update."
   * Comment: Comparing a method evaluated with 5x fewer trials against methods evaluated with 50 trials is methodologically inconsistent, since the variance of the DSRL success-rate estimate is substantially higher, making it easier for the DSRL numbers to appear artificially low or high by chance. This discrepancy directly affects the validity of Figure 7's core comparison, which the paper uses to argue that "DSRL achieves limited gains in our multi-task setting." Without matching evaluation budgets or providing confidence intervals proportional to trial count, it is not possible to conclude that DSRL genuinely underperforms VLAW rather than simply being noisily estimated. This weakens one of the paper's central claims about the superiority of the proposed approach over an alternative online RL baseline.

## Item 3: Reward model exhibits substantial unreliability that is not adequately addressed

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper's own validation of the reward model used to filter synthetic trajectories reveals a very high false-negative rate, which calls into question the quality and coverage of the synthetic training data central to the proposed method, yet this issue is not discussed as a limitation of the overall pipeline.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity; Data and methodology.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Ours (Probability Threshold p(yes) > 0.8) ... GT Success 10 12 ... Failure 2 16"
   * Comment: This confusion matrix, computed on only 40 manually labeled trajectories, shows that of the 22 ground-truth successful trajectories, 12 (54.5%) are misclassified as failures under the thresholded reward model used throughout the pipeline. Since this reward model is the sole mechanism for filtering synthetic and real rollouts into the positive training set (Eq. 3, Algorithm 1 steps 6 and 10), such a high false-negative rate implies that roughly half of genuinely successful synthetic trajectories are discarded, potentially biasing the training distribution and reducing the effective yield of useful synthetic data below what is implied elsewhere in the paper. Additionally, validating reward-model accuracy on only 40 trajectories is a very small sample from which to draw confident conclusions about reward reliability, and no discussion is provided regarding how this high FN rate might affect the diversity or coverage of the filtered synthetic dataset D+_syn used for policy fine-tuning.

## Item 4: Mismatch between the theoretical derivation and the actual algorithm implementation

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper provides a formal derivation connecting the policy update to regularized reinforcement learning with exponential advantage weighting, but the implemented algorithm uses a simple binary success/failure filter that is not a faithful instantiation of the derived weighting scheme, making the theoretical section largely decorative rather than justificatory.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions; Data and methodology.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "The weights are proportional to the exponential advantage: w(o, a) ∝ exp(A^{π_ref}(o,a)/β)."
   * Comment: This is the weighting scheme that Appendix A derives as the theoretically optimal projection under the regularized RL framework, requiring knowledge (or estimation) of a per-transition advantage function A^{π_ref}(o,a).
* Quote: "we assign a binary weight w(o, a) = 1 to transitions from successful trajectories and w(o, a) = 0 to transitions from failed trajectories"
   * Comment: The actual implementation collapses the continuous exponential-advantage weighting into a hard binary indicator based only on trajectory-level (not transition-level) success labels from the reward model, which is a much coarser heuristic equivalent to standard filtered behavior cloning. The paper's claim that "by setting the discount factor γ → 1 and assigning a large negative reward to failure trajectories, Eq. 11 reduces to Eq. 4" glosses over the fact that no advantage function is ever estimated or used anywhere in the pipeline, so the connection to the regularized RL framework is asserted rather than rigorously shown; this makes Section 4.3 read as post-hoc theoretical framing for what is in practice simple filtered supervised learning.

## Item 5: Numerical inconsistency between the abstract's headline result and the reported data

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The abstract's claimed "39.2% absolute success rate improvement" does not match the underlying success-rate values reported in the paper's own results table, raising concerns about the accuracy of the paper's headline quantitative claim.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions; Clarity and context.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "We achieve a 39.2% absolute success rate improvement over the base policy and 11.6% improvement from training with the generated synthetic rollouts."
   * Comment: Table 2 reports a mean base-model success rate of 0.460 and a mean "Ours-2" success rate of 0.868, giving an absolute improvement of 0.408, i.e., 40.8 percentage points, not 39.2%. While the 11.6% figure is consistent with the difference between Ours-2 (0.868) and Filtered BC-2 (0.752), the 39.2% figure cannot be reproduced from the per-task or mean values given anywhere in the main text, figures, or appendix tables. Such a discrepancy between the abstract's headline number and the supporting data undermines confidence in the precision of the paper's reported quantitative claims and should be clarified or corrected.

title: Cross-Domain Offline Policy Adaptation via Selective Transition Correction
review:
## Item 1: Theoretical guarantees are largely circular and provide limited insight

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The main theoretical results (Theorems 4.4–4.6) are derived from an assumption that essentially presupposes the very quantity of interest (the quality of the corrected transitions), making the theoretical contribution close to tautological rather than a substantive analysis of when/why the correction procedure works.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity; Conclusions (robustness and reliability of data interpretation).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Assumption 4.2. The estimated inverse policy model πˆinv well approximates the true empirical inverse policy model π tar inv such that the error between the empirical forward policy models in the corrected data and the target domain dataset is bounded, i.e., E [∥πˆ(s) − µtar(s)∥1] ≤ κ."
   * Comment: This assumption directly posits that the policy implied by the corrected data is close to the target behavior policy (bounded by κ), which is exactly the property that determines whether the correction procedure succeeds. The paper offers no analysis of how κ depends on controllable factors such as dataset size, network capacity, or the magnitude of the dynamics gap ε, so the assumption effectively assumes the desired outcome.
* Quote: "Theorem 4.4... the deviation between the corrected dynamics and the empirical target domain dynamics Pbtar(·|s, a) is bounded: ∥Pesrc(·|s, a) − Pbtar(·|s, a)∥ ≤ κ + ϵ." and "the following bound holds with probability at least 1 − δ: JMfsrc(π)−JMtar (π) ≥ − γrmax(κ + ϵ)/(1 − γ)^2 − C1√(1/n ln 2C2/δ)."
   * Comment: Both the dynamics-discrepancy bound and the finite-data performance bound are simply expressed in terms of the same unanalyzed κ from Assumption 4.2, so the theorems do not provide new quantitative insight into the actual behavior of the inverse-policy correction mechanism; they merely restate the assumption as an additive penalty term, limiting the practical value of the theoretical analysis for justifying the algorithm's design choices.

## Item 2: Mismatch between theoretical assumptions and the actual (deterministic) algorithm

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: Theorem 4.5, which is used to justify the reward-correction procedure, assumes a stochastic sampling process for the corrected action that does not match the deterministic action-correction rule actually used in the STC algorithm.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity; Conclusions.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Theorem 4.5. ... assume that the source domain rewards are corrected via rˆ(ssrc, asrc) = r(ssrc, asrc) + ∇ar(ssrc, a)⊤|a=asrc (ˆasrc − asrc), where aˆsrc ∼ µtar(·|ssrc)."
   * Comment: The theorem assumes the corrected action âsrc is a random sample drawn from the target behavior policy µtar, which would carry the full stochastic diversity of that policy.
* Quote: "aˆsrc = finv(ssrc, s′src)." (Eq. 2)
   * Comment: In the actual implementation, the corrected action is a deterministic output of the inverse policy network conditioned on (ssrc, s′src), not a stochastic draw from µtar. This discrepancy means the value-discrepancy bound in Theorem 4.5 does not rigorously apply to the algorithm as implemented, undermining the claimed theoretical justification for the reward-correction step.

## Item 3: The first-order Taylor reward correction is not validated for the magnitude of corrections it is applied to

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The reward correction relies on a local (first-order) Taylor approximation, which is only accurate for small action perturbations, yet the selective correction mechanism does not constrain the magnitude of the action change, so the approximation may be invalid precisely for the transitions that require the largest correction.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity; Data and methodology.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "we apply a first-order Taylor expansion around the original action to approximate the corrected reward... This correction leverages the local smoothness of the reward function in action space and enables efficient reward estimation without directly evaluating out-of-distribution (OOD) actions."
   * Comment: A first-order Taylor expansion is a local linear approximation whose accuracy degrades as ∥âsrc − asrc∥ grows; the paper provides no bound or check on this quantity before applying the approximation.
* Quote: "The corrected transition is adopted only if its dynamics discrepancy is substantially smaller than that of the original transition, formally defined as: τ˜src = (ssrc, aˆsrc, s′src, rˆsrc), if εcorr < λ · εorig..."
   * Comment: The acceptance criterion (Eq. 7) is based solely on the forward-dynamics discrepancy, not on the magnitude of the action change; therefore, large corrections (which are arguably the ones most needed under substantial dynamics mismatch) can be accepted even though the underlying Taylor-based reward estimate may no longer be locally valid, creating an unaddressed source of reward-estimation error for exactly the hardest cases the method targets.

## Item 4: Claim of "marginal" underperformance is not supported by the reported halfcheetah-morphology results

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper asserts that cases where STC underperforms baselines are marginal, but the reported results for halfcheetah under morphology shift show STC as the worst or near-worst performer with sizeable relative gaps and high variance, contradicting this claim.
* Evaluation criteria: Conclusions (robustness/validity of data interpretation); Clarity and context.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "While STC slightly underperforms other top-performing methods on several tasks, the gap is marginal and does not indicate a significant weakness."
   * Comment: This blanket claim is not consistent with the actual numbers reported for one full sub-domain of experiments.
* Quote (Table 1, Morph type): "half-med med 24.5±2.4 21.0±3.9 24.2±5.6 18.1±1.8 23.7±3.4 21.1±7.6 19.5±2.2" and "half-med-e med 21.1±2.8 19.2±2.2 23.2±3.9 21.1±1.9 18.6±1.3 20.8±2.5 16.8±8.8"
   * Comment: In these halfcheetah-morphology tasks, STC is the worst-performing method among all baselines (19.5 vs. best 24.5, and 16.8 vs. best 23.2), representing roughly 20–30% relative degradation rather than a marginal gap, and the STC result for half-med-e additionally shows a standard deviation (8.8) larger than half its mean, indicating high instability that is not discussed or explained anywhere in the main text or ablations, despite being a systematic pattern across all three source-data qualities for this task.

## Item 5: Asymmetric hyperparameter tuning between STC and several fixed-hyperparameter baselines

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: STC's key hyperparameters (λ, β) are swept and the best per-environment result is reported, whereas several baselines (IQL, DARA, BOSA) are run with a single fixed hyperparameter configuration across all tasks, which can bias the comparison in favor of STC.
* Evaluation criteria: Data and methodology (reproducibility/fairness of experimental comparison).

#### Evidence
* Quote: "For IQL, DARA, and BOSA, we employ a unified and fixed set of hyperparameters across all tasks."
   * Comment: These three baselines are evaluated without any task-specific tuning, meaning their reported scores reflect a single configuration that may not be optimal for each individual dynamics-shift/dataset-quality combination.
* Quote: "For STC, we fix the reward gradient coefficient α at 0.5, sweep the correction threshold λ over {1.0, 5.0}, and tune the Q-weighted loss coefficient β in the range {0.5, 5.0}, reporting the best result for each environment."
   * Comment: Reporting the best-performing configuration per environment for STC's two most important hyperparameters, while denying the same flexibility to IQL/DARA/BOSA, introduces an asymmetry that can inflate STC's apparent advantage over at least these baselines, making the total-score comparisons in Tables 1–3 less directly interpretable as a fair head-to-head comparison of the underlying methods.

title: Grounding Generated Videos in Feasible Plans via World Models
review:
## Item 1: Core video-guidance mechanism provides no benefit—or is harmful—in the paper's primary motivating scenario (zero-shot video plans)

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The central contribution of the paper (grounding video guidance via latent collocation) fails to demonstrate a benefit precisely in the zero-shot setting that motivates the entire work, both in the main comparison table and in the ablation study, which substantially weakens the paper's conclusions about the value of video guidance.
* Evaluation criteria: Validity; Conclusions and data interpretation.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "Removing video guidance by using random latent state initialization with λv = 0 affects performance differently depending on video quality. Specifically, it improves performance under zero-shot guidance (WAN-0S)... with success decreasing from 0.82 to 0.68 for domain-adapted videos (WAN-FT) and from 0.98 to 0.68 for oracle video plans."
   * Comment: This ablation (Table 4) shows that under WAN-0S, removing the paper's proposed video-guidance mechanism entirely (0.68) actually outperforms the full GVP-WM method (0.56). Since the paper repeatedly frames zero-shot video generation as the primary real-world use case ("particularly under out-of-distribution conditions"), a result where the core mechanism is actively harmful in this setting is a serious internal inconsistency that is not adequately addressed or explained in the main text.
* Quote: "Consequently, for WAN-0S, MPC-CEM performs better overall, except on Wall at T=50."
   * Comment: This statement from the main results section (Table 1) confirms that a simple world-model-only planner without any video guidance (MPC-CEM) generally outperforms GVP-WM when using zero-shot generated videos, which is the setting most reflective of real-world deployment (since domain-specific fine-tuning data or oracle expert videos will rarely be available). The paper's narrative frames GVP-WM as solving the problem of grounding "zero-shot image-to-video–generated" plans, yet the strongest baseline without any video guidance at all wins in this exact regime, undermining the claimed necessity and effectiveness of the proposed grounding method for its stated purpose.

## Item 2: Evaluation restricted to two simplistic, low-dimensional 2D simulation tasks

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The empirical validation is limited to two toy 2D environments (Push-T and Wall), which are far simpler than the real-world manipulation and navigation settings the paper's introduction and motivation target, limiting the generality and significance of the conclusions.
* Evaluation criteria: Originality and significance; Conclusions and data interpretation.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "We evaluate GVP-WM in two control environments across multiple long-horizon settings, following the evaluation protocols established in prior work [28]. Push-T [33] is a contact-rich 2D manipulation task... while Wall is a 2D navigation task that requires visual planning."
   * Comment: Both benchmark tasks are abstract 2D environments with simple rigid shapes rather than realistic 3D robotic manipulation or navigation scenes, which is a large gap from the motivating claims about "large-scale video generative models" being deployed as "zero-shot visual planners" for real robots. Given that the paper's introduction repeatedly emphasizes real-world physical feasibility and dynamics violations (e.g., "object teleportation," "motion blur" in realistic robotic contexts), demonstrating the method only on simplified 2D domains substantially limits the strength of claims about the method's broader applicability and significance to the wider robotics/planning community.
* Quote: "Future work includes extending GVP-WM to real-world robotic manipulation, where zero-shot video guidance is more likely to be in-distribution."
   * Comment: The authors themselves acknowledge that the current setting (simulated 2D tasks) is not representative of real-world manipulation, deferring the most convincing validation to future work, which suggests that the current empirical scope may be insufficient to support the paper's broad claims about grounding "large-scale video generative models" as practical zero-shot planners.

## Item 3: Absence of error bars, variance reporting, or statistical significance testing across stochastic components

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: Despite the method and baselines containing multiple sources of stochasticity (video diffusion sampling, ALM optimization with random initializations, and sampling-based local refinement), the paper reports only single-run point-estimate success rates on a small number of trials (50 episodes) without any confidence intervals, standard deviations, or repeated-seed analysis.
* Evaluation criteria: Appropriate use of statistics and treatment of uncertainties.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "For each setting, we evaluate on 50 initial–goal pairs sampled from expert policy trajectories of the corresponding horizon length. We report Success Rate, defined as the fraction of successful rollouts across all evaluation episodes."
   * Comment: With only 50 trials, the difference between reported success rates that differ by a few percentage points (e.g., 0.94 vs 0.86 in Table 1, or 0.68 vs 0.56 in Table 4) may fall well within sampling noise, yet no confidence intervals, standard errors, or multiple-seed repetitions are provided anywhere in the main text or appendices to substantiate that observed differences are statistically meaningful rather than due to chance in stochastic video generation, optimization initialization, or MPC sampling refinement (which explicitly involves random sampling: "sampling C candidate sequences from N (A∗, σ2I)").
* Quote: "we sample 500 samples with variance 0.3" (paraphrased from Appendix C.5 configuration details for local refinement)
   * Comment: This explicit stochastic sampling step in the pipeline, combined with the stochastic nature of diffusion-based video generation, means that repeated runs of the same experimental configuration could plausibly yield different success rates; without reporting variance across multiple seeds/runs, readers cannot assess whether the reported differences between methods (e.g., GVP-WM vs. MPC-CEM under WAN-0S) are robust or merely artifacts of a single stochastic realization.

* Main point of criticism: For the anticipating-lab-results and chest X-ray tasks—precisely the tasks where the paper reports its largest gains—the test set is artificially subsampled to a 50/50 class balance, which invalidates AUPRC as a measure of real-world clinical utility since AUPRC is highly sensitive to the underlying prevalence.

#### Evidence
* Quote: "For laboratory and chest X-ray tasks, which contain substantially more examples, we also subsample the training and test splits to include min(1000, n+) examples from each label."

Because AUPRC (unlike AUROC) is a direct function of prevalence, computing it on an artificially rebalanced test set produces a number that cannot be interpreted as an estimate of real deployment performance, contradicting the motivation given for choosing AUPRC in the first place.

title: Synapse Compendium Aware Federated Knowledge Exchange for Tool Routed LLMs
review:
## Item 1: Counterintuitive and internally inconsistent baseline results for "Centralized-SYNAPSE"

#### Claim
* Main point of criticism: The paper reports that the "Centralized-SYNAPSE" variant, which uses the exact same retrieval+rerank pipeline as the full system but with compendiums combined centrally (i.e., with full data access rather than federated approximation), performs dramatically *worse* than both the federated SYNAPSE and the simpler "Centralized-RetrievalOnly" ablation.
